nameStory: Lacy phacelia gets its delicate name from its finely divided, lace-like leaves that create an intricate, feathery pattern. The scientific name 'tanacetifolia' means 'tansy-leaved,' referring to how the foliage resembles the herb tansy with its deeply cut segments. This beautiful annual creates such delicate textures that it looks like nature's own lacework spread across the garden.
description: Lacy phacelia is a fast-growing annual flower that reaches about 2-3 feet tall with a bushy, upright habit. It produces masses of small, bell-shaped flowers in coiled clusters that unfurl like a fiddlehead fern, typically in shades of lavender-blue to purple. The plant's most distinctive feature is its deeply divided, fernlike leaves that give it a soft, delicate appearance. Originally from California, it's become popular as a garden annual and beneficial insect plant throughout New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small bell-shaped blooms in tight, coiled clusters that gradually unfurl in a spiral pattern, ranging from lavender-blue to deep purple with prominent white stamens that extend beyond the petals

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided, fernlike leaves that feel slightly rough and hairy to the touch, with narrow segments that create an intricate, lacy pattern

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright annual that grows 2-3 feet tall with multiple branching stems, creating a bushy appearance that's wider at the top

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Entire plant feels slightly fuzzy and rough due to fine hairs covering stems and leaves, with a distinctive herbaceous scent when brushed against

habitat: In New England, lacy phacelia is primarily found in cultivated gardens, particularly pollinator gardens and wildflower meadows where it's been intentionally planted. It occasionally escapes cultivation and can be found along disturbed edges, roadsides, and vacant lots, preferring well-drained soils in full sun locations.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring after soil warms, with young plants showing their characteristic lacy foliage first.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period from mid-summer through early fall, with the distinctive coiled flower clusters most prominent and attractive to pollinators.
seasonality.fall: Continues blooming until first frost, then plants die back completely as seeds mature and drop.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground presence as this annual dies completely, surviving only as seeds that may germinate the following spring.

funFact: Lacy phacelia is considered one of the world's best bee plants, capable of supporting up to 1,000 pounds of honey production per acre - that's why commercial beekeepers often plant entire fields of it as 'bee pasture'!
confusionNotes: The coiled flower clusters might remind you of forget-me-nots or other borage family members, but lacy phacelia's deeply divided, fernlike leaves are the giveaway - most similar flowers have simple, undivided leaves.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'fiddleneck' in the UK, this plant is different from the toxic fiddleneck (Amsinckia species) found in western North America. Also note that while it's in the borage family, some sources may list it under the older family name Hydrophyllaceae, which has been merged into Boraginaceae in modern classification systems.
compareHints: Lacy phacelia stands out from its relatives desert bluebells and Miami Mist primarily by its deeply divided, lacy leaves - the other phacelias have simpler, less dissected foliage. Desert bluebells has broader, bell-shaped flowers in bright blue, while Miami Mist has smaller, more delicate blooms, but neither has the intricate leaf structure of lacy phacelia.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Desert bluebells stand out from their Phacelia relatives by their incredibly intense blue color and bell-shaped flowers.
Miami Mist differs from its relatives like Lacy Phacelia in having much smaller, more delicate flowers and a more sprawling growth habit.
